title: Support Vector Machines
text:
Overview
These are notes are designed to aid the material for the SVM section of the course. They are neither the exclusive nor exhaustive material. They may include content which is beyond the scope or expectation of the course. These sections should, hopefully, be pointed out in lectures. They are adapted from the material delivered by Dr. Sebnem Er in the past.
Additional resources are:
as well as those provided on Amathuba.

title: Support Vector Machines
text:
0.1 What Is Included
These notes cover:

maximal margin classifiers
support vectors and margins
soft-margin classifiers and slack variables
the cost parameter
nonlinear decision boundaries
feature expansion and kernels
practical implementation in R with e1071
tuning and interpretation

The mathematics of SVMs is still present, but is not covered in any rigour. These notes keep the formal setup because it helps explain why SVMs work. An appendix is included to aid here. If there are any concepts you feel are necessary to add, please let me know.

title: Support Vector Machines
text:
0.2 Practical Notes

The full worked R examples are included directly in the relevant chapters.
These examples are written to be self-contained.

title: 2  A Brief Overview
text:
2.1 Support Vector Machines
A Support Vector Machine (SVM) is a classification model that chooses a decision boundary by balancing two goals: separating the classes correctly and keeping a wide buffer around the boundary. That buffer is known as the margin.
Under an ideal scenario, the model chooses the separating boundary which correctly classifies each training data point with the largest margin. Under less perfect cases, it allows some margin violations when that gives a boundary that is more stable and likely to generalise better.
SVMs are useful because they connect three ideas cleanly:

title: 2  A Brief Overview
text:
classification through finding a boundary
generalisation by keeping a margin away from the nearest training points
flexibility through feature transformations and kernels

title: 2  A Brief Overview
text:
2.2 Main Goals
By the end of the topic, you should be able to answer the following:
Geometry and optimisation:

What does an SVM optimise?
Why are support vectors important?

Tuning and practice:

What does the cost parameter do?
How can we tune the cost parameter?

Extensions and relevance:

How do kernels allow nonlinear classification?
When might SVMs be a good classification model choice?

title: 2  A Brief Overview
text:
2.3 The Basic Problem
Suppose that we have a binary classification problem where each observation has a predictor vector \(x_i \in \mathbb{R}^p\) and class label \(y_i \in \{-1, +1\}\).
An SVM classifier creates a score function, \(f:\mathbb{R}^p \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\), with the form
\[f(\mathbf{x}) =  \mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + b.\] Classification of observations is based on the signed outcome of the score function.
At its core, the SVM creates a boundary where this expression equals zero: \[\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + b = 0.\] Here \(w\) is the vector of coefficients that controls the orientation of the boundary, and \(b\) is the scalar intercept that shifts the boundary.
Geometrically, \(f(\mathbf{x})\) is a signed side-of-boundary score. Its sign tells us which side of the boundary the point \(\mathbf{x}\) is on; whereby \(f(\mathbf{x})=0\) means the point lies exactly on the boundary.
The traditional SVM structure for binary classes can be extended to multiclass problems by combining several binary SVMs; however, these are beyond the scope of this course.

title: 2  A Brief Overview
text:
2.4 Primary Intuition
Consider a simple 2D example where the two classes are linearly separable, such as that shown in Figure 2.1. Based on the observations, we can easily find a boundary line which perfectly separates the points into their correct classes. In fact, there are infinitely many of these lines; however, we do not want just any separating line. We want one that leaves a wide gap between the two classes. A wider gap improves the generalisation of the model for classifying future points into their correct class. That gap is known as the margin.








Figure 2.1: A simple 2D example illustrating potential separating boundary lines.





We will solidify the following ideas:

not all separating boundaries are equally good
the best linear boundary is the one with the largest margin
only a few points determine that boundary

Only the closest observations can shrink the margin. Points far inside their own class could move slightly without changing the chosen boundary. The closest, boundary-defining observations are known as the support vectors.

title: 3  Maximal Margin Classifier
text:
3.1 A 1D Opener
The maximal margin classifier is the boundary that defines the classification rule which
Hence, the use of this classifier requires that the observations are separable. We will build up the intuition for the classifier from 1D to \(p\)-dimensions.

title: 3  Maximal Margin Classifier
text:
3.1.1 Intuition
Let us begin with the simplest binary classification case; one predictor and two classes that can be perfectly separated on a line. For this reason, consider the Figure 3.1. Since the groups on the left and right are perfectly separated; then many boundaries could correctly classify each observation in the training data. In fact, there are infinitely many since any boundary \(c \in [-1.9, 3.0]\) would perfectly separate the groups. A natural question arises: Which threshold should we choose?
The SVM approach is to choose the boundary that is as far as possible from the nearest point in either class.


3.1.2 Formal Statement
When we talk about finding a boundary to separate the observations, we are implicitly trying to make a decision rule. We want to define some value \(c\) such that \[\begin{equation}
  \begin{cases}
    x_i \leq c \hskip{2em} x_i\rightarrow \text{group 1}\\
    x_i > c \hskip{2em} x_i\rightarrow \text{group 2}
  \end{cases}
\end{equation}\]
In one dimension, the decision boundary is just the value \(c\) which is a point on \(\mathbb{R}\). Trivially, if the the closest points from the two classes are at \(l\) and \(u\), then the maximal-margin boundary, \(c\), lies halfway between them such that
\[
c = \frac{l + u}{2}.
\]
This is the simplest version of the SVM idea. Such a decision rule

correctly classifies
keeps the boundary far from the training data
lets the nearest observations determine the rule









Figure 3.1: In one dimension, many thresholds work, but the maximal margin boundary sits halfway across the widest gap between the classes.

title: 3  Maximal Margin Classifier
text:
3.2 Building the mechanics in 2D
Extending the predictor set to 2-dimensions means that the decision boundary is a line instead of a point. We continue with the natural extension of the ideas established in the 1D case without restricting ourselves to just two dimensions. This will allow us to build intuition in a feasible manner.

3.2.1 Intuition
Once again, consider the example illustrated by Figure 3.2. It is clear that there are infinitely-many lines that can separate the classes of the training data perfectly. The maximal margin classifier chooses the line with the widest empty strip around it. That strip is bounded by two parallel lines touching the nearest observations in each class.








Figure 3.2: In two dimensions, several separating lines may classify the training points correctly. The SVM idea is to prefer the line with the widest empty strip around it.





Therefore, the maximal margin classifier requires us to find the optimal gradient and intercept for the decision boundary line.


3.2.2 The Mathematical Outline
Whilst we could set up the mathematics for a line in 2-dimensions; we can consider a hyperplane in \(p\)-dimensions from the start. That is because a \(p\)-dimensional hyperplane can be defined by the equation
\[
\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + b = 0.
\] In 1D this is a point; in 2D, a line; 3D a plane; and a hyperplane in higher dimensions. Here \(\mathbf{w}\) is a vector which is normal (perpendicular) with respect to the boundary and \(b\) is a scalar which shifts the decision boundary away from the origin. Therefore, we use this equation to define the decision boundary. This boundary defines our decision rule.
In particular, for any observation \(x_i\), compute the score
\[
s_i = \mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + b.
\]
The score tells us which side of the boundary the point is on:

\(s_i > 0\): positive side of the boundary
\(s_i < 0\): negative side of the boundary
\(s_i = 0\): exactly on the boundary







NoteBack to 1D…





In one dimension, this is especially concrete. If
\[
w_1 x + b = 0,
\]
then the boundary point is
\[
x = -\frac{b}{w_1}.
\]
Checking the sign of \(w_1 x + b\) is therefore a way of checking whether \(x\) is on one side or the other of that boundary point. In higher dimensions the same idea holds, except the boundary is a line, plane, or hyperplane rather than a single point.



In an attempt to find the maximal margin, let us attach class labels \(y_i \in \{-1,+1\}\) for each observation. Without loss of generality, we can choose the positive side of the boundary to correspond to class \(+1\) and the negative side to correspond to class \(-1\).
That gives two separate correct-classification conditions:



True class
Desired side
Condition




\(y_i = +1\)
positive side
\(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + b > 0\)


\(y_i = -1\)
negative side
\(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + b < 0\)



Two inequalities are still messy to work with; hence, we can collapse both of these rows into one expression. If \(y_i = +1\), multiplying the condition by \(y_i\) leaves the score unchanged. If \(y_i = -1\), multiplying the condition by \(y_i\) flips the sign, so a negative score becomes positive.
Therefore correct classification means \[
y_i(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + b) > 0
\] for every training point.
Finally, we can let \[
y_i(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + b) = 1
\] represent the margin line.
The maximal margin classifier requires us to combine these components; solving the optimisation problem
\[
\min_{b,w} \frac{1}{2}\lVert w \rVert^2
\]
subject to
\[
y_i(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + b) \geq 1, \qquad i = 1,\dots,n.
\]
The optimal solutions for \(\mathbf{w}\) and \(b\) have the following form \[
\mathbf{w} = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i y_i \mathbf{x}_i,
\]
\[
b = y_k - \mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}_k,
\] for any \(k\) such that \(\alpha_k \neq 0\). Furthermore, the score function has the form \[
f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i y_i \mathbf{x}_i \cdot \mathbf{x} + b.
\] Noting that the function is controlled by a dot product on \(\mathbf{x}\) alone will become a critical characteristic later on; but we will get there…


3.2.3 A Summary of the Mathematics
The above mathematics simply formalises the following geometric approach of SVMs:

we constrain the maximal margin boundary to correctly classify with a buffer
the buffer size is proportional to \(1/\lVert w \rVert\)
minimising \(\lVert w \rVert^2\) is equivalent to maximising the margin

Hence, the optimisation problem is just a precise way to say; find the separating hyperplane with the biggest safety gap around it.

title: 3  Maximal Margin Classifier
text:
3.3 Support Vectors
At this point, we have established the mechanics of the support vector machine, not just in 2D, but in \(p\)-dimensions. We outlined the mathematics to find this optimal maximal margin boundary; but what is a support vector?
One can easily see that most observations do not affect the optimal boundary once it has been found. Points far from the boundary can move around without changing the classifier at all. In fact, the important points are the ones that lie on the margin, those are the points which define the optimal boundary, they “support” the boundary. Hence, they are known as the support vectors.
Recall that we can characterise observations that lie on the margin as those which satisfy the equation
\[
y_i(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + b) = 1.
\] Another characterisation is provided by the values of \(\alpha_i\) which are nonzero. The correspond point \(\mathbf{x}_i\) is a support vector. (See optimisation block below for more information.)
Support vectors are the training points that carry the geometric information needed to define the classifier machinery, hence the name support vector machines.





The separating line is pinned down by the observations touching the margins. Those highlighted points are the support vectors.










NoteA little more about the optimisation





The maximal margin problem is characterised by

an objective which is convex
constraints that are linear

In optimisation language, this implies that the solution can be expressed through a dual problem. This dual can be represented as \[
\max \sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i - \frac{1}{2}\sum_i\sum_j \alpha_i\alpha_jy_i\mathbf{x}_i\cdot\mathbf{x}_j
\] such that \[
\sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0,
\] \[
\qquad \alpha_i \geq 0, \qquad \forall i\in\{1, \dots, n\}.
\]
The dual representation derives the solution form shown above,
\[
\mathbf{w} = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i y_i \mathbf{x}_i,
\]
where nonzero \(\alpha_i\) values correspond to support vectors.
This explains why support vectors are special in the optimisation language:

if \(\alpha_i = 0\), that observation does not affect the fitted boundary
if \(\alpha_i > 0\), that observation is actively shaping the classifier

title: 3  Maximal Margin Classifier
text:
3.4 The Convex Hull Approach
Another way to think about the maximal margin classifier is through the perspective of convex hulls which makes the dual optimisation problem more intuitive. A convex hull is the smallest convex region containing a set of points. (See the appendix for a fuller explanation)
The process for finding the maximal margin classifier can be viewed as

finding the closest pair of points, one on each class’s convex hull
connecting pair with a vector, which is normal to the separating boundary
placing the optimal boundary through the midpoint of this hull-connecting vector

For each of the connecting points of the two hulls, the points are defined by a weighted average of observations from its class. These observations are the support vectors since the boundary is determined by the nearest points between the two class hulls, and these nearest points are defined by the support vectors. This idea is illustrated in Figure 3.3.








Figure 3.3: A convex-hull approach to the maximal margin classifier.

title: 3  Maximal Margin Classifier
section: 3.5 Another Dimension: Does it still work?
text:
3.5 Another Dimension: Does it still work?
Consider the following 3D example. In the two-dimensional projection illustrated in Figure 3.4, we can see that the two classes are not linearly separable, there is significant class overlap. With our current mechanics, the data appears to be incompatible with the SVM approach.








Figure 3.4: In the two-dimensional projection, the two classes overlap heavily.





However, once we include a third predictor, the same observations are easy to separate linearly with a plane.




After adding the third predictor, an interactive 3D view shows a simple separating plane at \(x_3 = 0\).


Nothing conceptually new happens in three dimensions. A line in 2D becomes a plane in 3D, and more generally a hyperplane in \(p\) dimensions. The same margin logic still applies and the mathematics we established above is generalised to any dimension.

title: 3  Maximal Margin Classifier
text:
3.6 R Example: Separable Iris Case
Let us use the Iris dataset to illustrate the maximal margin classifier process in R. We will consider subsets of the Iris data that give a clean first look at thresholds, support vectors, and the fitted margin.
For this example, we keep only two species so that the example is genuinely binary.


Show iris setup code
library(ggplot2)
library(e1071)

data(iris)

iris_bin <- subset(iris, Species != "virginica")
iris_bin$Species <- droplevels(iris_bin$Species)

table(iris_bin$Species)



3.6.1 Find the 1D maximal margin boundary using Petal Length
Let us begin with the easiest case, one dimension. Analysing the data, it is clear that the classes are separable with just Petal Length. Here, the decision boundary is just a threshold value which completely defines the classification decision rule.


Show 1D iris threshold code
threshold_info <- data.frame(
  max_setosa = max(iris_bin$Petal.Length[iris_bin$Species == "setosa"]),
  min_versicolor = min(iris_bin$Petal.Length[iris_bin$Species == "versicolor"])
)
threshold_info$threshold <- mean(c(
  threshold_info$max_setosa,
  threshold_info$min_versicolor
))

ggplot(iris_bin, aes(x = Petal.Length, y = 0, color = Species)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = threshold_info$threshold, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "1D separation by threshold", y = NULL)





A one-dimensional threshold separates the two iris species cleanly using petal length.






3.6.2 Expand to 2D classification by including Petal Width
The two-dimensional version is closer to the SVM geometry we have spent a lot of time on: a threshold becomes a line, and the margin becomes a parallel strip around that line. Figure 3.5 shows that the 2D subset is linearly separable. Now we need to see how to find the optimal boundary.


Show 2D iris plot code
p2 <- ggplot(iris_bin, aes(x = Petal.Width, y = Petal.Length, color = Species)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Scatterplot of Iris subset")
p2








Figure 3.5: Using petal width and petal length, the two selected iris species are linearly separable.






3.6.2.1 Fit the Linear SVM
To fit an SVM model to the data, we utilise e1071::svm. The function expects:

formula: identifies the classes and predictors for the model. (Can use x and y instead of the formula approach)
data: the dataset which the model references.
type: the SVM machinery has been extended to more than just classification. In this course, we discuss the C-classification type. This is the default type if the response variable is a factor.
kernel: this will make more sense in chapter 5. Until then, we utilise the linear kernel.
scale: whether to standardise the preidctor variables before fitting the SVM.
cost: this will become clear in chapter 4. If you want to use a maximal margin classifier, then set a relatively large cost.

The fitted model identifies the support vectors in addition to the characterisation of the optimal boundary.


Show SVM fit code
svm_model <- svm(
  Species ~ Petal.Width + Petal.Length,
  data = iris_bin,
  type = "C-classification",
  kernel = "linear",
  scale = FALSE,
  cost = 10
)


pred <- predict(svm_model, iris_bin)
data.frame(
  training_accuracy = mean(pred == iris_bin$Species),
  support_vectors = length(svm_model$index)
)




3.6.2.2 Inspect the Support Vectors
Recall that the support vectors are the observations that lie on the boundary. They are the points that determine where the final separating line sits.


Show support vector extraction code
support_df <- iris_bin[svm_model$index, ] # This shows the observations from the iris_bin dataset which are the support vectors of the SVM.


We can then use this support vector information to indicate which data points are the support vectors.


Show support-vector plot code
p3 <- p2 +
  geom_point(
    data = support_df,
    aes(x = Petal.Width, y = Petal.Length),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    color = "black",
    size = 5,
    alpha = 0.25
  ) +
  labs(title = "Which observations are support vectors?")
p3








Figure 3.6: The highlighted observations are the support vectors used to pin down the fitted boundary.







3.6.2.3 Draw the Boundary and Margins
The fitted linear SVM gives a separating line and two parallel margin lines. We can use the SVM information to plot these two lines, fully visualising the 2D maximal margin classification.


Show boundary and margin plotting code
w <- as.numeric(t(svm_model$coefs) %*% svm_model$SV)
slope <- -w[1] / w[2]
intercept <- svm_model$rho / w[2]

p4 <- p3 +
  geom_abline(slope = slope, intercept = intercept) +
  geom_abline(slope = slope, intercept = intercept + 1 / w[2], linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_abline(slope = slope, intercept = intercept - 1 / w[2], linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Decision boundary and margins")
print(p4)








Figure 3.7: The fitted SVM boundary and margins for the separable iris example.







3.6.2.4 Extrapolating the predictions
We can also visualise the classification by plotting the model.


Show model plot code
plot(svm_model, iris_bin[, c("Petal.Width", "Petal.Length", "Species")])








Figure 3.8: The prediction space of the SVM model.





However, due to the resolution of the plot, the boundary line appears rather jagged. We could add shading to our previous plot to show the prediction space a little better (although not necessary).


Show model ggPlot code
# Build a grid over the predictor space
xRange <- range(iris_bin$Petal.Width)
yRange <- range(iris_bin$Petal.Length)

xPad <- 0.15 * diff(xRange)
yPad <- 0.15 * diff(yRange)

gridDf <- expand.grid(
  Petal.Width = seq(xRange[1] - xPad, xRange[2] + xPad, length.out = 300),
  Petal.Length = seq(yRange[1] - yPad, yRange[2] + yPad, length.out = 300)
)

# Predict the class on the grid
gridDf$PredictedClass <- predict(svm_model, newdata = gridDf)

p4_shaded <- p4 +
  geom_raster(
    data = gridDf,
    aes(x = Petal.Width, y = Petal.Length, fill = PredictedClass),
    alpha = 0.15,
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Decision boundary, margins, and predicted regions",
    fill = "Predicted class"
  )
print(p4_shaded)








Figure 3.9: The prediction space of the SVM model, but with ggPlot.

title: 3  Maximal Margin Classifier
text:
3.7 Takeaway
The maximal margin classifier is the clean starting point for understanding SVMs:

it is geometrically intuitive
it shows why support vectors matter
it motivates the optimisation problem naturally
BUT it requires perfect separation which is often too restrictive for real data

title: 4  Soft-Margin Classifier
text: 4.1 Why Perfect Separation Is Too Fragile

title: 4  Soft-Margin Classifier
text:
4.1.1 Intuition
Real data are rarely perfectly separable. Even if they are, a single unusual point can make the maximal margin classifier unstable.
That means the perfectly separating solution can overreact to noise. In practice we often prefer a boundary that allows a few violations if it leads to a more stable and more useful classifier.
This is the move from the maximal margin classifier to the soft-margin classifier.





The soft-margin idea becomes necessary as soon as a perfectly separating boundary is either impossible or too unstable to trust.

title: 4  Soft-Margin Classifier
text:
4.2 The Main Idea
The goal is no longer:

classify every training point correctly at all costs

The new goal is:

allow some mistakes or margin violations if that gives a better overall boundary

title: 4  Soft-Margin Classifier
text:
4.3 Slack Variables

4.3.1 Intuition
We need a way to measure how badly a point violates the margin condition. Slack variables do exactly that.

a point outside the margin has no violation
a point inside the margin has a positive violation
a misclassified point has an even larger violation



4.3.2 Formal Statement
Introduce slack variables \(\xi_i \geq 0\). The soft-margin optimisation problem becomes
\[
\min_{b,w,\xi} \frac{1}{2}\lVert w \rVert^2 + C \sum_{i=1}^n \xi_i
\]
subject to
\[
y_i(b + w^\top x_i) \geq 1 - \xi_i, \qquad i = 1,\dots,n
\]
and
\[
\xi_i \geq 0.
\]


4.3.3 Interpretation
The objective has two competing pieces:

\(\frac{1}{2}\lVert w \rVert^2\) wants a wide margin
\(C \sum \xi_i\) penalises violations

So the soft-margin classifier balances two priorities:

keep the boundary simple and wide
avoid too many or too severe classification violations






Slack variables encode how badly a point violates the margin condition: inside-margin points are tolerated, while wrong-side points incur larger penalties.

title: 4  Soft-Margin Classifier
text:
4.4 What the Slack Variable Means
The usual interpretation is:

\(\xi_i = 0\): correctly classified and outside or on the margin
\(0 < \xi_i \leq 1\): correctly classified, but inside the margin
\(\xi_i > 1\): misclassified

title: 4  Soft-Margin Classifier
text:
4.5 The Cost Parameter

4.5.1 Intuition
The parameter cost in e1071::svm() controls how harshly margin violations are penalised.
In the mathematical objective, this is the role of \(C\):
\[
\frac{1}{2}\lVert w \rVert^2 + C \sum_{i=1}^n \xi_i.
\]
The first term wants a wide, simple margin. The second term penalises violations. The cost parameter controls how much we care about the second term relative to the first.


4.5.2 Interpretation

high cost: fewer violations tolerated, tighter fit, lower bias, higher variance
low cost: more violations tolerated, smoother boundary, higher bias, lower variance

This is one of the most important practical tuning ideas in SVMs.





Schematic: changing the cost parameter changes the tradeoff. Low cost allows a wider, more forgiving boundary; high cost pushes harder against violations.

title: 4  Soft-Margin Classifier
section: 4.6 Support Vectors in the Soft-Margin Case
text:
4.6 Support Vectors in the Soft-Margin Case
The support vectors are now the observations that lie:

exactly on the margin
inside the margin
or on the wrong side of the boundary

These are the points that determine the solution. Observations far away from the boundary still matter little.

title: 4  Soft-Margin Classifier
text:
4.7 Cost Versus Errors
Students often confuse the goal of a high-cost SVM with “fewer training errors means better model”. That is too simplistic.
A very high cost may reduce training error while harming generalisation. A softer classifier can perform better on new data because it is less sensitive to individual observations.
This is the usual bias-variance tradeoff:

if cost is too small, the model is too forgiving and may underfit
if cost is too large, the model chases individual training points and may overfit
the best value is usually somewhere in the middle, and we estimate it using validation performance

title: 4  Soft-Margin Classifier
text:
4.8 Cross-Validation for Cost Tuning
Cross-validation gives a practical way to choose cost without using the test set.
The workflow is:

Choose a grid of candidate cost values.
Split the training data into folds.
For each cost, repeatedly fit on all but one fold and evaluate on the held-out fold.
Average the held-out errors across folds.
Choose the cost with the best average validation performance.
Refit the final model on the full training data using that chosen cost.

The key point is that cross-validation estimates generalisation error, not training error. Training error usually improves as the model becomes more flexible, but validation error can get worse once the model starts overfitting.

title: 4  Soft-Margin Classifier
text:
4.9 R Example: Simulated Linear Overlap
This example deliberately creates two overlapping classes. A hard-margin classifier is not appropriate here, so the focus is on how cost changes the soft-margin fit.

4.9.1 Simulate the Data
The two classes overlap, so no straight line can separate every point cleanly.


Show soft-margin simulation code
library(ggplot2)
library(e1071)

set.seed(42)
n <- 120

# Two overlapping Gaussian clouds for a clean soft-margin example.
class0 <- data.frame(
  x1 = rnorm(n / 2, mean = 0.0, sd = 0.85),
  x2 = rnorm(n / 2, mean = 0.2, sd = 0.85),
  class = factor("red", levels = c("red", "blue"))
)

class1 <- data.frame(
  x1 = rnorm(n / 2, mean = 1.2, sd = 0.85),
  x2 = rnorm(n / 2, mean = 1.0, sd = 0.85),
  class = factor("blue", levels = c("red", "blue"))
)

dat <- rbind(class0, class1)

ggplot(dat, aes(x = x1, y = x2, color = class)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "blue")) +
  labs(title = "Overlapping classes: soft margin setting")





The simulated classes overlap, which motivates the soft-margin classifier.






4.9.2 Fit Several Cost Values
Smaller cost values tolerate more margin violations. Larger cost values push harder against violations and can reduce training error, but that does not automatically mean better test-set performance.


Show cost comparison code
fit_with_cost <- function(cost_value) {
  svm(
    class ~ x1 + x2,
    data = dat,
    type = "C-classification",
    kernel = "linear",
    scale = FALSE,
    cost = cost_value
  )
}

model_low <- fit_with_cost(0.2)
model_mid <- fit_with_cost(1)
model_high <- fit_with_cost(20)

cost_models <- list(
  "0.2" = model_low,
  "1" = model_mid,
  "20" = model_high
)

data.frame(
  cost = c(0.2, 1, 20),
  training_accuracy = unname(vapply(
    cost_models,
    function(model) mean(predict(model, dat) == dat$class),
    numeric(1)
  )),
  support_vectors = c(
    length(model_low$index),
    length(model_mid$index),
    length(model_high$index)
  )
)


  cost training_accuracy support_vectors
1  0.2         0.7833333              71
2  1.0         0.7916667              62
3 20.0         0.8000000              59


The training accuracy increases slightly as cost increases, but this is not enough to choose the model. A higher-cost model is being rewarded for fitting the training data more tightly, so we need cross-validation to check whether that tighter fit generalises.


4.9.3 Inspect One Fitted Model
For the middle cost value, we can inspect the training accuracy and the points that act as support vectors.


Show accuracy and support-vector summary code
pred_mid <- predict(model_mid, dat)

sv_df <- dat[model_mid$index, ]

data.frame(
  cost = 1,
  training_accuracy = mean(pred_mid == dat$class),
  support_vectors = nrow(sv_df)
)


  cost training_accuracy support_vectors
1    1         0.7916667              62




Show soft-margin support-vector plot code
p <- ggplot(dat, aes(x = x1, y = x2, color = class)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "blue")) +
  labs(title = "Overlapping classes: soft margin setting")

p2 <- p +
  geom_point(
    data = sv_df,
    aes(x = x1, y = x2),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    color = "darkgreen",
    size = 5,
    alpha = 0.25
  ) +
  labs(title = "Support vectors for cost = 1")
p2





Support vectors for the fitted soft-margin classifier with cost equal to 1.






4.9.4 Draw the Boundary and Margins
The margin lines now act as a soft buffer. Some observations are allowed to fall inside the buffer or even on the wrong side.


Show soft-margin boundary plotting code
w <- as.numeric(t(model_mid$coefs) %*% model_mid$SV)
slope <- -w[1] / w[2]
intercept <- model_mid$rho / w[2]

p3 <- p2 +
  geom_abline(slope = slope, intercept = intercept) +
  geom_abline(slope = slope, intercept = intercept + 1 / w[2], linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_abline(slope = slope, intercept = intercept - 1 / w[2], linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Soft-margin boundary and margins")
p3





The fitted soft-margin boundary and margins for cost equal to 1.

title: 4  Soft-Margin Classifier
text:
4.10 Tuning in R
The tune.svm() function is useful here because it makes the bias-variance tradeoff tangible. It fits the model repeatedly across a grid of cost values and estimates how well each value performs on held-out folds.
For teaching, a fine regular grid is easy to read. In larger applications, it is common to start with a wider grid on a log scale, such as 2^(-5:5), then refine around the promising values.


Show tune.svm code
set.seed(123)

tuned <- tune.svm(
  class ~ x1 + x2,
  data = dat,
  kernel = "linear",
  cost = seq(0.05, 5, by = 0.05),
  tunecontrol = tune.control(cross = 10)
)

tuning_results <- tuned$performances

data.frame(
  best_cost = tuned$best.parameters$cost,
  best_cross_validation_error = tuned$best.performance
)


  best_cost best_cross_validation_error
1       0.1                         0.2


The table above gives the selected value. The curve below is usually more informative because it shows whether the choice is sharp or whether several nearby values perform similarly.


Show cross-validation curve code
ggplot(tuning_results, aes(x = cost, y = error)) +
  geom_line(color = "#0072B2", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2", size = 1.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = tuned$best.parameters$cost, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate(
    "label",
    x = tuned$best.parameters$cost,
    y = min(tuning_results$error),
    label = paste("best cost =", tuned$best.parameters$cost),
    hjust = -0.05,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Cost",
    y = "10-fold cross-validation error",
    title = "Choosing cost by cross-validation"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)





Cross-validation error across candidate cost values. The selected cost is the value with the lowest average held-out error.




When explaining this plot, focus on the shape rather than only the minimum. If the curve is flat near the minimum, then several cost values are performing almost equally well. In that situation, a simpler or softer choice is often easier to justify than an aggressively high-cost model.

4.10.1 Takeaway
The soft-margin classifier is the practical version of the maximal margin idea:

it keeps the margin principle
it tolerates imperfect separation
it introduces a tunable tradeoff through cost
cross-validation chooses cost using held-out performance rather than training error

title: 5  Nonlinear SVMs
text: 5.1 Why Linear Boundaries Are Not Enough

title: 5  Nonlinear SVMs
text:
5.1.1 Intuition
Sometimes the classes are clearly structured but not linearly separable in the original feature space. A straight line or flat hyperplane is then the wrong tool.
This does not mean the SVM idea breaks down. It means we need a richer representation of the predictors.

title: 5  Nonlinear SVMs
text:
5.2 Feature Expansion

5.2.1 Intuition
A nonlinear problem in the original variables may become linear after transforming the predictors.
Examples:

add squared terms
add interactions
add cubic terms

The boundary can then be linear in the transformed space even though it is nonlinear in the original space.


5.2.2 Formal Statement
Let \(\phi(x)\) be a transformation into a higher-dimensional feature space. Then the classifier takes the form
\[
f(x) = b + w^\top \phi(x).
\]


5.2.3 Interpretation
The model is still a linear separator, but it is linear in the transformed feature space rather than in the original predictors.





A one-dimensional problem that is not separable by one threshold can become separable after mapping from \(x\) to \(x^2\).

title: 5  Nonlinear SVMs
section: 5.3 Why Not Just Keep Adding Features?
text:
5.3 Why Not Just Keep Adding Features?
In principle we could create large polynomial expansions directly. In practice this becomes computationally expensive and awkward very quickly.
This is where kernels enter.

title: 5  Nonlinear SVMs
text:
5.4 Kernel Idea

5.4.1 Intuition
The SVM optimisation can be written in a way that depends on observations only through inner products. If we can compute inner products in the transformed space without explicitly constructing all transformed features, we get the benefit of feature expansion more efficiently.
This is the key bridge from the support vector classifier to the support vector machine. The linear classifier can be written using training observations rather than an explicit coefficient vector. The only operation we need between two observations is an inner product.
This is also why the dual representation appears here. The point is not to spend time deriving the dual problem in detail. The point is to show that the final classifier can be written entirely in terms of similarities between observations. Once that is true, we can replace ordinary inner products with kernel functions.


5.4.2 Formal Statement
For the linear support vector classifier, the fitted coefficient vector can be written as
\[
w = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i y_i x_i.
\]
Substituting this into the linear decision function gives
\[
f(x) = b + w^\top x
     = b + \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i y_i x_i^\top x.
\]
Only observations with \(\alpha_i > 0\) contribute to this sum. These are the support vectors.
If we first transform the predictors using \(\phi(x)\), the same algebra becomes
\[
f(x) = b + \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i y_i \phi(x_i)^\top \phi(x).
\]
A kernel function is
\[
K(x_i, x_j) = \phi(x_i)^\top \phi(x_j).
\]
The decision function can be written as
\[
f(x) = b + \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i y_i K(x, x_i).
\]


5.4.3 Interpretation
The kernel trick is therefore a substitution:
\[
x_i^\top x_j
\quad\text{is replaced by}\quad
K(x_i, x_j).
\]
This lets us work as if we had transformed the data, without explicitly building the full transformed feature set. The appendix gives the supporting inner-product algebra and a worked polynomial-kernel expansion.

title: 5  Nonlinear SVMs
text:
5.5 Common Kernels

5.5.1 Linear kernel
\[
K(x_i, x_j) = x_i^\top x_j
\]
Use when a linear boundary is plausible.


5.5.2 Polynomial kernel
\[
K(x_i, x_j) = (c + x_i^\top x_j)^d
\]
Useful when curved interactions of moderate complexity are expected. The appendix works through the common teaching example with \(c = 2\) and \(d = 2\).


5.5.3 Radial kernel
\[
K(x_i, x_j) = \exp(-\gamma \lVert x_i - x_j \rVert^2)
\]
This is often a strong general-purpose choice because it can represent flexible local boundaries.


5.5.4 Sigmoid kernel
\[
K(x_i, x_j) = \tanh(\kappa x_i^\top x_j + c)
\]
The sigmoid kernel is related to neural-network-style activations. In practice, it is less commonly the default teaching choice than the linear, polynomial, or radial kernels.

title: 5  Nonlinear SVMs
text:
5.6 Kernel Notation in e1071
The mathematical notation above is the clean conceptual version. The e1071::svm() arguments use slightly different names:

kernel = "linear" corresponds to \(K(x_i, x_j) = x_i^\top x_j\)
kernel = "polynomial" uses degree, gamma, and coef0, roughly \((\text{gamma} \, x_i^\top x_j + \text{coef0})^{\text{degree}}\)
kernel = "radial" uses gamma in \(\exp(-\gamma \lVert x_i - x_j \rVert^2)\)
kernel = "sigmoid" uses gamma and coef0 inside a hyperbolic tangent

This is a notation issue rather than a conceptual difference. In class, the important idea is still that the kernel controls the similarity calculation.

title: 5  Nonlinear SVMs
text:
5.7 What Gamma Does
For the radial kernel:

large \(\gamma\): very local influence, more flexible boundary
small \(\gamma\): smoother and broader influence, less flexible boundary

So radial SVM tuning usually involves both cost and gamma.





A radial kernel is really a similarity rule. Larger gamma makes similarity decay much faster with distance.

title: 5  Nonlinear SVMs
text:
5.8 Which Kernel Should We Use?
There is no universal rule. Kernel choice depends on:

the shape of the class boundary
the amount of training data
the scale and meaning of the predictors
empirical validation performance

That is why tuning and visual interpretation matter.

title: 5  Nonlinear SVMs
text:
5.9 Simple Nonlinear Teaching Examples
This section uses two teaching routes:

explicit feature expansion
kernel-based fitting

This sequence works well because students first see why the transformed space helps, and only then see how kernels avoid manual expansion.





In the original space, a ring-shaped class structure is clearly nonlinear. A straight line can split the ring, but it cannot separate the centre from the outer ring.




A useful way to understand the kernel idea is to imagine lifting the original data into a space with extra coordinates. For the ring example, one natural extra coordinate is
\[
r^2 = x_1^2 + x_2^2.
\]
In the original \((x_1,x_2)\) plot, inner and outer points form concentric rings. In the lifted \((x_1,x_2,r^2)\) view, inner points have small \(r^2\) and outer points have large \(r^2\), so a flat plane can separate them.
For this teaching example, we can think of the feature map as
\[
\phi(x) = (x_1, x_2, x_1^2 + x_2^2).
\]
A linear rule in this lifted space can be as simple as
\[
f(\phi(x)) = x_1^2 + x_2^2 - 2.
\]
That is a plane in the lifted space. When projected back down to the original \((x_1,x_2)\) space, the same rule becomes a circular boundary.




A nonlinear pattern in the original variables can become linearly separable after lifting the data into a feature space.


This is the core intuition behind kernels. A kernel lets the SVM behave as if it had access to a richer feature space, but without manually constructing every transformed variable.
In the dual form, the SVM only needs inner products between transformed observations:
\[
\phi(x_i)^\top \phi(x_j).
\]
The kernel replaces that calculation with
\[
K(x_i, x_j).
\]
So the visual story is: the original data are hard to separate, a lifted feature space makes the separation linear, and the kernel gives the SVM access to that lifted-space geometry through similarity calculations. The radial kernel does not literally add only the single coordinate \(x_1^2+x_2^2\); its feature space is richer than this. The 3D lift is a teaching analogy that makes the mechanism visible.





After a simple transformation, the same pattern can be separated with a linear boundary. This is the core feature-expansion idea.

title: 5  Nonlinear SVMs
text:
5.10 R Example: Ring Data
This example compares three strategies on the same ring-shaped data:

a linear kernel on the original variables
a linear kernel after explicit feature expansion
a radial kernel on the original variables


5.10.1 Simulate and Split the Data
The training data have an inner class and an outer class. The structure is obvious visually, but it is not linearly separable in the two original coordinates.


Show ring data setup code
library(ggplot2)
library(e1071)

set.seed(7)
n_inner <- 80
n_outer <- 120

make_ring <- function(n, radius_mean, radius_sd, label) {
  angle <- runif(n, 0, 2 * pi)
  radius <- rnorm(n, mean = radius_mean, sd = radius_sd)
  data.frame(
    x1 = radius * cos(angle),
    x2 = radius * sin(angle),
    class = factor(label, levels = c("inner", "outer"))
  )
}

inner <- make_ring(n_inner, 0.8, 0.10, "inner")
outer <- make_ring(n_outer, 2.0, 0.20, "outer")
data_ring <- rbind(inner, outer)

set.seed(7)
train_index <- sample(seq_len(nrow(data_ring)), size = round(0.8 * nrow(data_ring)))
traindf <- data_ring[train_index, ]
testdf <- data_ring[-train_index, ]

ggplot(traindf, aes(x = x1, y = x2, color = class)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.75) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Ring data: nonlinear boundary in the original space")





The ring data are nonlinear in the original two-dimensional predictor space.






5.10.2 Linear Kernel on the Original Variables
A linear kernel only has access to straight-line separation in the original predictor space, so it is the wrong model for this geometry.


Show linear-kernel fit code
linear_model <- svm(
  class ~ x1 + x2,
  data = traindf,
  type = "C-classification",
  kernel = "linear",
  scale = TRUE,
  cost = 1
)

data.frame(
  model = "linear kernel on original variables",
  train_accuracy = mean(predict(linear_model, traindf) == traindf$class),
  test_accuracy = mean(predict(linear_model, testdf) == testdf$class)
)


                                model train_accuracy test_accuracy
1 linear kernel on original variables        0.60625         0.575




5.10.3 Linear Kernel After Explicit Feature Expansion
If we add squared terms, the ring structure becomes easier for a linear classifier to represent.


Show expanded-feature fit code
traindf$x1_sq <- traindf$x1^2
traindf$x2_sq <- traindf$x2^2
testdf$x1_sq <- testdf$x1^2
testdf$x2_sq <- testdf$x2^2

expanded_model <- svm(
  class ~ x1_sq + x2_sq,
  data = traindf,
  type = "C-classification",
  kernel = "linear",
  scale = TRUE,
  cost = 1
)

data.frame(
  model = "linear kernel on squared variables",
  train_accuracy = mean(predict(expanded_model, traindf) == traindf$class),
  test_accuracy = mean(predict(expanded_model, testdf) == testdf$class)
)


                               model train_accuracy test_accuracy
1 linear kernel on squared variables              1             1




5.10.4 Radial Kernel on the Original Variables
The radial kernel lets the SVM behave as if it is using a richer feature space, without manually adding the squared variables.


Show radial-kernel fit code
radial_model <- svm(
  class ~ x1 + x2,
  data = traindf,
  type = "C-classification",
  kernel = "radial",
  scale = TRUE,
  cost = 1,
  gamma = 0.5
)

data.frame(
  model = "radial kernel on original variables",
  train_accuracy = mean(predict(radial_model, traindf) == traindf$class),
  test_accuracy = mean(predict(radial_model, testdf) == testdf$class)
)


                                model train_accuracy test_accuracy
1 radial kernel on original variables              1             1




Show radial-kernel boundary plot code
plot(radial_model, traindf[, c("x1", "x2", "class")])





The radial kernel produces a nonlinear boundary in the original two-dimensional space.






5.10.5 Tune the Radial Kernel
The radial kernel has both cost and gamma to tune. Here we use a small grid to show the workflow.


Show radial-kernel tuning code
tuned <- tune.svm(
  class ~ x1 + x2,
  data = traindf,
  kernel = "radial",
  cost = seq(0.1, 2, by = 0.1),
  gamma = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1)
)

data.frame(
  best_cost = tuned$best.parameters$cost,
  best_gamma = tuned$best.parameters$gamma,
  best_cross_validation_error = tuned$best.performance
)


  best_cost best_gamma best_cross_validation_error
1       0.1       0.25                           0

title: 5  Nonlinear SVMs
section: 5.11 Practical Comparison to Show in Class
text:
5.11 Practical Comparison to Show in Class
With the ring example, it is useful to contrast:

linear kernel on original variables
linear kernel on transformed variables
radial kernel on original variables

That sequence makes the kernel idea feel necessary rather than decorative.

5.11.1 Takeaway
Nonlinear SVMs do not replace the linear story. They extend it:

the optimisation logic stays the same
the boundary is still linear in some feature space
kernels let us work in that richer space efficiently

title: 6  Applications, Comparisons, and Extensions
text:
6.1 Where SVMs Work Well
SVMs are often effective when:

title: 6  Applications, Comparisons, and Extensions
text:
classes are reasonably well separated
predictor dimension is moderate to high
the decision boundary is important, but probability estimation is not the main goal
a carefully tuned nonlinear classifier may outperform simpler linear methods

title: 6  Applications, Comparisons, and Extensions
text:
6.2 Comparison to Other Methods
The following table is a useful closing reference for students when deciding whether an SVM is a sensible modelling choice.












Method
Main Strength
Main Limitation
Probability Output
Nonlinear Boundaries
Scaling Sensitivity
Tuning Burden




Logistic regression

Relies on distributional assumptions

6.2.1 SVM versus Logistic Regression
Logistic regression is usually preferable when:

probabilities are central
coefficient interpretation matters
a simple linear decision rule is adequate

SVMs are often attractive when:

classification accuracy is the main concern
margin-based robustness is useful
nonlinear boundaries are important



6.2.2 SVM versus LDA
LDA works well under stronger distributional assumptions. If those assumptions are reasonable, it can be very effective. SVMs are less assumption-driven and often more flexible, especially in nonlinear settings.

title: 6  Applications, Comparisons, and Extensions
text:
6.3 Important Practical Limits
Students should leave with a balanced view:

SVMs can perform very well
they are not automatically interpretable
kernel choice and tuning matter
feature scaling is usually important
probability output is not their main strength

title: 6  Applications, Comparisons, and Extensions
text:
6.4 Extensions Mentioned Briefly
There are several related SVM extensions. It is enough to name them here without treating them in detail:

support vector regression
novelty or outlier detection
variable selection variants
boosting-related uses
density estimation links
feature detection
clustering variants

title: 6  Applications, Comparisons, and Extensions
text:
6.5 Final Summary
The conceptual arc of SVMs is:

start with the best separating boundary
replace perfect separation with a soft margin
move from linear to nonlinear boundaries through transformations
use kernels to do this efficiently

title: Appendix A — Concepts Appendix
text:
A.1 Convex Hulls
This appendix collects short explanations of ideas that support the SVM material, but would interrupt the main flow if explained fully at the first point of use.

title: Appendix A — Concepts Appendix
text:
A.1.1 Intuition
Take a set of points drawn on a page. Imagine stretching a rubber band around the outside of those points and then letting it tighten. The shape enclosed by the rubber band is the convex hull of the points.
The convex hull includes:

the original points
the straight-line edges between the outermost points
every point inside the enclosed region

The key word is convex. A region is convex if the straight line between any two points in the region also stays inside the region.


A.1.2 Formal Definition
For points \(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n\), the convex hull is the set of all convex combinations:
\[
\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i x_i :
\lambda_i \geq 0,\ \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i = 1 \right\}.
\]
The weights \(\lambda_i\) are non-negative and add to one. This means a convex combination is a weighted average of the original points.


A.1.3 Why It Matters for SVMs
For a linearly separable two-class problem, each class has its own convex hull. If the two convex hulls do not overlap, then there is at least one separating hyperplane between the classes.
The maximal-margin classifier can be understood geometrically as finding the separating boundary halfway between the closest parts of the two class hulls. This is why points deep inside each class usually do not affect the boundary: they are not close to the other class hull.
The support vectors are the observed points that lie on or near those closest parts. They are the points that determine where the margin sits.

title: Appendix A — Concepts Appendix
section: A.2 Primal and Dual SVM Problems
text:
A.2 Primal and Dual SVM Problems

A.2.1 Intuition
The word dual sounds more abstract than it needs to. In optimisation, a dual problem is a different way of writing the same optimisation task.
For SVMs, the direct or primal problem asks:

Which boundary should we choose?

The dual problem asks a different but equivalent question:

Which training points should be allowed to influence the boundary, and by how much?

This is why the dual form is useful for teaching SVMs. It connects the optimisation directly to support vectors.


A.2.2 The Primal Problem
For the hard-margin classifier, the primal problem is
\[
\min_{b,w} \frac{1}{2}\lVert w \rVert^2
\]
subject to
\[
y_i(b + w^\top x_i) \geq 1,
\qquad i = 1,\dots,n.
\]
This says:

choose the boundary parameters \(b\) and \(w\)
classify every training point correctly
make the margin as wide as possible

So the primal is the most direct mathematical version of the geometric story.


A.2.3 From Constraints to Multipliers
The primal problem has one margin constraint for each training observation. The dual introduces one multiplier, \(\alpha_i\), for each of these constraints.
The multiplier \(\alpha_i\) measures how much the \(i\)th observation matters to the final boundary.
This gives the key interpretation:

if \(\alpha_i = 0\), the observation has no direct influence on the boundary
if \(\alpha_i > 0\), the observation is active in determining the boundary

The active observations are the support vectors.


A.2.4 The Hard-Margin Dual
For the hard-margin SVM, the dual problem can be written as
\[
\max_{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n}
\left[
\sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i
- \frac{1}{2}
\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n
\alpha_i \alpha_j y_i y_j x_i^\top x_j
\right]
\]
subject to
\[
\alpha_i \geq 0,
\qquad i = 1,\dots,n,
\]
and
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i y_i = 0.
\]
The details of this optimisation are less important than the structure. The dual uses:

the class labels \(y_i\)
the multipliers \(\alpha_i\)
inner products between pairs of observations, \(x_i^\top x_j\)

It no longer directly optimises over \(w\).


A.2.5 Recovering the Boundary
After solving the dual, the boundary coefficient vector is recovered as
\[
w = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i y_i x_i.
\]
This equation is central to the SVM story. It says the fitted boundary is built as a weighted combination of training observations.
Most observations get \(\alpha_i = 0\), so they disappear from the sum. The remaining observations, with \(\alpha_i > 0\), are the support vectors.
This is the optimisation reason why support vectors matter.


A.2.6 Why Positive \(\alpha_i\) Means Support Vector
The SVM solution satisfies a condition called complementary slackness. For the hard-margin case, it implies
\[
\alpha_i\left[y_i(b + w^\top x_i) - 1\right] = 0.
\]
This product can be zero in two ways:

\(\alpha_i = 0\), so the point does not influence the solution
\(y_i(b + w^\top x_i) = 1\), so the point lies exactly on the margin

Therefore, if \(\alpha_i > 0\), the point must lie on the margin. These are exactly the support vectors in the hard-margin picture.


A.2.7 Soft-Margin Dual
The soft-margin classifier keeps the same idea but allows margin violations. In the primal, this is done with slack variables \(\xi_i\) and a cost parameter \(C\).
In the dual, the main change is a new upper bound on the multipliers:
\[
0 \leq \alpha_i \leq C.
\]
The interpretation is:

\(\alpha_i = 0\): the point is outside the margin and does not shape the boundary
\(0 < \alpha_i < C\): the point lies on the margin
\(\alpha_i = C\): the point is inside the margin or on the wrong side

So the soft-margin dual still identifies the observations that matter, but it also reflects how strongly violations are penalised.


A.2.8 Why the Dual Enables Kernels
The most important practical reason for the dual is that the dual objective contains observations only through inner products:
\[
x_i^\top x_j.
\]
If we transform the data using \(\phi(x)\), the dual would use
\[
\phi(x_i)^\top \phi(x_j).
\]
A kernel computes this transformed inner product directly:
\[
K(x_i, x_j) = \phi(x_i)^\top \phi(x_j).
\]
This is why kernels are possible. We do not need to explicitly build all transformed features. We only need to compute the inner products that the dual asks for.


A.2.9 Teaching Summary
For lecture purposes, the dual has three main roles:

it explains why only support vectors determine the classifier
it rewrites the classifier in terms of similarities between observations
it creates the opening for the kernel trick

The algebra is important, but the intuition is more important: the primal chooses the boundary directly; the dual discovers which observations are responsible for that boundary.

title: Appendix A — Concepts Appendix
section: A.3 Inner Products and Kernel Algebra
text:
A.3 Inner Products and Kernel Algebra

A.3.1 Why Inner Products Matter
Inner products deserve a short aside because they are the algebraic reason kernels work.
An inner product, also called a dot product or scalar product, combines two vectors into a single number. For two vectors \(x\) and \(z\) with \(p\) components,
\[
x^\top z = \sum_{j=1}^p x_j z_j.
\]
This number is useful because it contains geometric information. It can also be written as
\[
x^\top z = \lVert x \rVert \lVert z \rVert \cos(\theta),
\]
where \(\theta\) is the angle between the two vectors.
This gives the intuition:

if \(x\) and \(z\) point in a similar direction, the inner product is large and positive
if they point in opposite directions, the inner product is negative
if they are orthogonal, the inner product is zero

So an inner product is not just algebra. It is a simple similarity measure.


A.3.2 The Linear SVM Written With Inner Products
A linear SVM classifies using
\[
f(x) = b + w^\top x.
\]
From the dual optimisation problem, the fitted coefficient vector can be written as a weighted sum of the training observations:
\[
w = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i y_i x_i.
\]
Substituting this expression for \(w\) gives
\[
f(x)
= b + \left(\sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i y_i x_i\right)^\top x.
\]
Using the distributive rule,
\[
f(x)
= b + \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i y_i x_i^\top x.
\]
This is the important step. The classifier compares a new point \(x\) with each training point \(x_i\) only through the inner product \(x_i^\top x\).
In practice, many \(\alpha_i\) values are zero. The nonzero terms correspond to the support vectors, so the classifier can be written as
\[
f(x)
= b + \sum_{i \in S} \alpha_i y_i x_i^\top x,
\]
where \(S\) is the set of support vectors.
The predicted class is determined by the sign of \(f(x)\).


A.3.3 Moving to a Transformed Feature Space
Suppose we transform the original predictors using a feature map \(\phi(x)\). A linear classifier in that transformed space is
\[
f(x) = b + w^\top \phi(x).
\]
The same dual argument gives
\[
w = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i y_i \phi(x_i).
\]
Substituting again,
\[
f(x)
= b + \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i y_i \phi(x_i)^\top \phi(x).
\]
This is the support vector machine version of the support vector classifier. The only change is that the inner product is now taken after transforming the observations.


A.3.4 The Kernel Trick
A kernel is a function that computes an inner product in the transformed space:
\[
K(x_i, x)
= \phi(x_i)^\top \phi(x).
\]
So instead of explicitly constructing \(\phi(x)\), we use
\[
f(x)
= b + \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i y_i K(x_i, x).
\]
This is the kernel trick:
\[
\phi(x_i)^\top \phi(x)
\quad\text{is computed through}\quad
K(x_i, x).
\]
The teaching point is that the model behaves as if it is fitting a linear separator in a richer feature space, but the computation can be done using only kernel values.


A.3.5 Worked Polynomial Kernel Example
Take two observations with two predictors:
\[
x = (x_1, x_2),
\qquad
z = (z_1, z_2).
\]
Consider the degree-two polynomial kernel with constant \(c = 2\):
\[
K(x,z) = (2 + x^\top z)^2.
\]
Since
\[
x^\top z = x_1z_1 + x_2z_2,
\]
we get
\[
K(x,z)
= (2 + x_1z_1 + x_2z_2)^2.
\]
Expanding the square:
\[
K(x,z)
= 4 + 4x_1z_1 + 4x_2z_2
  + x_1^2z_1^2 + 2x_1x_2z_1z_2 + x_2^2z_2^2.
\]
This expanded expression is an inner product in a transformed feature space. One valid feature map is
\[
\phi(x) =
\left(
2,\,
2x_1,\,
2x_2,\,
x_1^2,\,
\sqrt{2}x_1x_2,\,
x_2^2
\right).
\]
Then
\[
\phi(x)^\top \phi(z)
= 4 + 4x_1z_1 + 4x_2z_2
  + x_1^2z_1^2 + 2x_1x_2z_1z_2 + x_2^2z_2^2.
\]
So
\[
K(x,z) = \phi(x)^\top \phi(z).
\]
The important lesson is not this specific feature map. The important lesson is that the kernel computes the same value we would get after expanding the features, but without requiring us to build every transformed variable manually.


A.3.6 Radial Kernel as Similarity
The radial basis kernel is
\[
K(x,z) = \exp(-\gamma \lVert x-z \rVert^2).
\]
If \(x\) and \(z\) are close together, then \(\lVert x-z \rVert^2\) is small, so \(K(x,z)\) is close to one. If they are far apart, then \(K(x,z)\) is close to zero.
This is why the radial kernel is often explained as a local similarity rule. The parameter \(\gamma\) controls how quickly similarity decays with distance.
